title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Petrochemical Plants | PT
description: Dye penetrant inspection for US chemical plants: stainless, duplex, nickel, titanium and zirconium with halogen-controlled materials. Request a PT quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Petrochemical and Chemical Plants in the US
html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to US petrochemical, polymer and specialty chemical plants for liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, of stainless steel, duplex, nickel alloy and titanium or zirconium equipment, plus small fittings and weld repairs on any metal. Penetrant reveals cracks and porosity that are open to the surface. We use materials controlled for halogens and sulfur, and we clean up so product contact surfaces stay clean. Request a PT inspection quote with your component list.

Why chemical plants lean on penetrant

A chemical complex is full of metals that magnets ignore. Stainless steels carry corrosive acids, caustic and solvents; duplex grades handle chlorides; nickel alloys resist hot acids; titanium and zirconium appear in acid and oxidizing service. None of these respond to magnetic particle inspection, so liquid penetrant is the main surface method for them. It is also the practical choice for small, awkward parts, such as instrument connections and socket-welded fittings, where a yoke cannot reach. For carbon steel, magnetic particle is usually quicker; MT for petrochemical plants covers that. Penetrant finds only surface-open flaws, so thickness and internal weld quality go to UT for petrochemical plants.

Where PT is asked for in chemical service

  • Stainless and duplex piping welds. New construction, tie-ins and repairs on process lines. The owner's piping specification, built on ASME B31.3, names the examination and extent.
  • Heat exchangers. Tube-to-tubesheet welds, channel and shell welds and repair areas, usually examined while the bundle is out. Cleanliness of the tube bore matters, so cleaning is planned carefully.
  • Stainless and alloy vessels and reactors. Nozzle welds, internal attachment welds and clad or overlay areas, examined at turnarounds or after repairs.
  • Chloride-exposed stainless. Piping and vessels near cooling-water or under wet insulation, where branched cracking can start from the outside.
  • Titanium and zirconium equipment. Acid-service vessels and exchangers, where the penetrant itself must be free of halogens.
  • Pump, valve and machinery repairs. Casing weld repairs, seat buildup and shaft-adjacent weld repairs, where a surface crack means rejection.
  • Sanitary and high-purity systems. Piping and vessels built to ASME BPE or similar owner standards in specialty chemical, food-grade and pharmaceutical-adjacent plants, with strict control of residues.

The scope in each case is set by the owner's inspector or engineer, working within OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 mechanical integrity requirements and EPA 40 CFR Part 68 where the process is covered. Related pages go deeper on stainless steel penetrant testing and weld penetrant testing.

How we keep penetrant from harming the equipment

The materials matter as much as the method. Penetrant, cleaner and developer for austenitic stainless, nickel alloys, titanium and zirconium must be certified low in chlorine, fluorine and sulfur, with the controls described in ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165. We use certified batches, record the lot numbers on the report, and bring the supplier's analysis if the owner wants to see it. After the examination, we remove developer and penetrant residue with approved cleaner so nothing is left in crevices or on surfaces that touch product. Where the owner has a stricter written limit on halogens, solvents or particulates, send it with the request and we will build the procedure around it.

Solvent cleaners and aerosol penetrants are flammable, so the site's hot work and ventilation rules apply, and we tell the permit writer exactly what we carry.

Steps of a field test

  1. Preparation. Grind or clean to bare, smooth metal and remove oil, paint, flux and product residue. A weld that was blasted or ground heavily can smear metal over a crack and close it, so we ask for a light etch or cleaner step when the surface has been worked.
  2. Apply. Visible red-dye penetrant is sprayed or brushed over the area with a margin, and kept wet for the full dwell time.
  3. Remove. Excess penetrant is wiped with a dry, then lightly solvent-damp, lint-free cloth. Direct solvent spray would wash penetrant out of flaws.
  4. Develop. A thin coat of white developer draws penetrant from open flaws and magnifies the indication.
  5. Interpret. The technician examines the surface within the time window in the procedure, under the light level Article 6 requires, and records relevant indications.
  6. Clean. Remaining developer and penetrant are removed and the area is left ready for coating, insulation or product.

The Level II technician records metal temperature, because the standard technique has a limited temperature range. A line in hot sun or on a cold winter morning may fall outside it; in that case a qualified alternate technique has to be demonstrated first.

Heat exchanger welds and the cleanliness problem

Exchangers in chemical service are among the most common penetrant jobs, and also among the trickiest. Tube-to-tubesheet welds sit in a dense field of small welds, each with a crevice behind it, and any penetrant that seeps into that crevice is difficult to flush out. We therefore control how much material goes on, keep the wipe-off disciplined, and agree with the owner how the bundle will be cleaned and tested after the examination. Where a hydrostatic or leak test follows, the sequence matters, because a test can push residual penetrant to the surface and make clean welds appear to bleed. We will recommend an order of operations and put it on the report.

Preparation mistakes that hide cracks

Most missed indications trace back to preparation rather than to the penetrant itself. Grinding, wire brushing and blasting can smear metal across the opening of a tight crack and close it. Oil, grease and product residue fill the flaw before penetrant can enter. Paint and heavy oxide seal the surface. For stainless, even a cleaning cloth carrying the wrong solvent can leave a film. Our procedure therefore calls for cleaning appropriate to the contamination, a controlled solvent, a complete dry before application, and a light etch where the surface has been mechanically worked and the owner allows it. If a surface is not fit for examination we stop and say so instead of reporting an absence of flaws on a surface that could not show them.

The same goes for chemical plants where product residue may be hazardous. Decontamination, flushing and sign-off by the owner's operations team come before our crew touches the equipment, and we do not work on surfaces still wet with process fluid.

Penetrant or something else

When PT is the right and wrong choice in a chemical plant
SituationBetter methodReason
Weld on 316 stainless linePTNot magnetic
Weld on carbon steel sphereMTFaster, also sees shallow subsurface flaws
Cracks beneath an overlay or deep in a weldUTPT sees only the surface
Wall loss at an elbowUTPT cannot measure thickness
Rough, porous or heavily coated surfacePrepare first, then PT or MTSurface must be clean and smooth

When the surface is porous, such as some castings and rough weld cap profiles, penetrant can leave a lot of background bleed-out, and magnetic particle or UT may do better. Our MT versus PT guide and the Article 6 explainer go through these calls in detail.

Acceptance and records

Acceptance criteria come from the construction or repair code named in the procedure: ASME B31.3 for piping, Section VIII for vessels, or the owner's specification for specialty equipment. The Level II technician reports the position and size of every relevant indication and records the criteria cited. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report before it is issued. The owner's inspector decides whether a flaw is repaired, monitored or investigated further. We do not set remaining life or fitness-for-service conclusions; that remains with your engineer.

Planning in an operating complex

Technicians travel to your site and are mobilized for the agreed scope. Plants with toxic or reactive chemicals impose their own entry rules: gas monitors, restrictions on clothing, escorts, rules on what can be carried in, and, near ports, TWIC. Heat exchanger and vessel work usually coincides with an outage, so share the shutdown sequence and tell us when surfaces will be clean and accessible. Weather matters outdoors: rain and wind affect dwell, wiping and development, and we may need a tent or a pause. Scaffold access, insulation removal and cleaning are arranged by the owner's crew. See the pressure vessel inspection page and the turnaround page for how scopes fit around outages.

What the PT report contains

  • Equipment tag, weld or component ID and location on the drawing.
  • Procedure number and revision, code section and acceptance criteria cited.
  • Product names, batch numbers and halogen or sulfur certificates for the penetrant materials used.
  • Surface preparation, metal temperature, dwell and development times, and light level.
  • Name and level of the technician, with the ASNT Level III reviewer.
  • Indications by type, size and position, a sketch or photograph, and accept or reject.
  • Cleanup steps completed after the test.

What to send us for a quote

  • Component list, drawings or a weld map with tags.
  • Materials by grade, including any titanium, zirconium or nickel alloys.
  • Quantity, size and surface condition; any heavy grinding or blasting.
  • Governing code or specification, and any limits on halogens, sulfur or solvent residue.
  • Metal temperature range, insulation, coatings and access needs.
  • Site address, credentials, safety orientation and the work window.

Where we work in the US for chemical plants

  • Houston: stainless and alloy equipment in Ship Channel chemical plants.
  • Beaumont: polymer and chemical plants of Southeast Texas.
  • Baton Rouge: chemicals and fertilizer on the river corridor.
  • Lake Charles: large chemical and olefins sites.
  • Corpus Christi: coastal chemical facilities.
  • New Orleans: river chemical plants and storage terminals.
  • Louisville: specialty chemical plants on the Ohio River.
  • Chicago: Great Lakes chemical and polymer plants.

Training your own technicians

For in-house penetrant capability, see PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 training, along with the penetrant testing simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A your company certifies its personnel from its own written practice, and our written practice development service supports that. The manufacturing NDT training page outlines sector programs, and the national penetrant testing page gives an overview.

Scope limits to know about

We do not perform radiographic work in the United States, and specialist techniques fall outside what this page covers. Alloy identification and the authorized inspector's role stay with others. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

faq.q: Can you do penetrant testing on titanium or zirconium equipment?
faq.a: Yes, using penetrant, cleaner and developer certified low in halogens and sulfur, with batch numbers recorded on the report. We confirm any additional site limits before the work starts.

faq.q: What do you need to quote PT in a chemical plant?
faq.a: A component or weld list, grades of material, quantity, governing code, surface condition, metal temperature range, access, chemical limits and your work window. Tell us if the equipment sees high-purity service.

The owner's inspector or engineer accepts or rejects them against the code criteria named in the procedure. Our technician reports each indication, and an ASNT Level III reviews the report before it goes out.
Controlled materials and a full cleanup step prevent that. We remove penetrant and developer, record the cleanup on the report, and follow any written residue limit from your plant.

faq.q: Can PT find cracks under an overlay or deep inside a weld?
faq.a: No. Penetrant sees only flaws open to the surface. Internal weld flaws and wall loss are for ultrasonic testing, and carbon steel surface cracks are often faster with magnetic particle.

faq.q: Does penetrant work on hot or cold equipment?
faq.a: Only within the temperature range in the procedure. Outside it, a modified technique has to be demonstrated, so tell us the metal temperature before scheduling.

faq.q: Is penetrant testing the same as dye penetrant inspection?
faq.a: Yes. Liquid penetrant testing, dye penetrant inspection and PT are different names for the same method. We usually use visible red dye in the field and fluorescent only when the specification calls for it.

faq.q: Do you handle pump or valve weld repairs?
faq.a: Yes, as part of a repair scope, including casing welds and seat buildup. We examine the weld area and report indications for your inspector to disposition.

faq.q: Do your technicians travel outside the Gulf Coast?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your site anywhere in the United States, including Kentucky and the Great Lakes states, with lead time depending on site credentials and permits.
